faq.a: For moderate‑severe disease, high‑risk patients (immunocompromised, pregnant) or when symptoms last >48 h.
faq.q: When should I give antibiotics for traveller’s diarrhoea?

faq.a: Yes, it is category B and preferred over fluoroquinolones for pregnant travelers.
Treat empirically based on likely pathogens; use azithromycin or ciprofloxacin according to local resistance patterns.
faq.q: What if I have no access to stool culture?

exam: What clinical features differentiate invasive bacterial diarrhoea from typical traveller’s diarrhoea? — Look for blood/mucus, high fever, severe abdominal pain; invasive pathogens produce leukocytes in stool.

How would you manage a child with severe dehydration from traveller’s diarrhoea in a clinic without IV fluids? — Give rapid ORS via nasogastric tube or syringe feeding; seek transfer if unable to correct dehydration.
Why is ciprofloxacin avoided in a pregnant traveler with diarrhoea? — Fluoroquinolones cross the placenta and are associated with cartilage toxicity in the fetus.
When should you suspect a parasitic cause and change therapy? — Persistent diarrhoea >2 weeks, travel to endemic areas, or stool antigen positive for Giardia; switch to metronidazole or tinidazole.
What red‑flag sign mandates immediate referral to a higher‑level facility? — Signs of shock (hypotension, tachycardia, cold extremities) or severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs.
Explain why rifaximin is not suitable for dysentery. — It is non‑systemic and does not reach invasive organisms causing blood/mucus; ineffective against Shigella or Campylobacter.
How does the WHO dehydration scale guide fluid therapy? — Classifies dehydration as none, some, or severe; dictates ORS volume or need for IV crystalloids.
ai.title: Traveller's Diarrhoea
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Acute diarrhoea acquired during travel, usually bacterial, is managed with rehydration, selective antibiotics and supportive care. Severity, likely pathogen and resource limits guide treatment in low‑resource settings.

b: Onset within 1 week of arrival
No chronic gastrointestinal disease history
sections.p: Acute onset of ≥3 loose stools in 24 h after travel to a region with poor sanitation, lasting <14 days. Diagnosis is clinical; stool culture is optional when available.

b: Mild: <5 stools/24 h, no dehydration
Moderate: 5‑10 stools/24 h, some dehydration
Severe: >10 stools/24 h, profuse vomiting, signs of shock
sections.p: Severity guides therapy. Use the WHO dehydration scale and the clinical severity score (mild, moderate, severe).

b: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) – most frequent
Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC)
Campylobacter jejuni
Shigella spp.
Non‑typhoidal Salmonella
Viral: Norovirus, Rotavirus
Protozoa: Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica (in longer trips)
Consider HIV‑related opportunistic diarrhoea in high‑risk travelers
sections.p: Most cases are bacterial; viral and parasitic causes are less common but important in immunocompromised travelers.

b: Stools without blood or mucus in typical bacterial TD
Fever ≤38.5 °C common with ETEC, Campylobacter
Blood/mucus suggests invasive bacteria (Shigella, Campylobacter) or dysentery
sections.p: Frequent watery or semi‑liquid stools, abdominal cramps, nausea, low‑grade fever; may have vomiting. In severe disease, signs of dehydration dominate.

t.a: Stool microscopy and culture (if lab exists)
t.b: Identify bacterial pathogen → guides targeted antibiotic; negative culture does not rule out ETEC
Detects protozoal infection → treat with metronidazole; not needed in typical short‑term TD
Presence suggests invasive bacteria (Shigella, Campylobacter); absence supports non‑invasive ETEC
Assess dehydration severity; if unavailable, use clinical signs (dry mucosa, tachycardia, hypotension)

b: Severe dehydration or shock
Persistent high fever >38.5 °C >48 h
Bloody stools or severe abdominal pain
Signs of sepsis (tachypnoea, altered mental status)
Immunocompromise (HIV, chemotherapy)
sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent referral or inpatient care.

b: Oral rehydration solution (ORS) – 75 ml/kg over 4 h for moderate dehydration
IV crystalloids (Ringer's lactate) if unable to tolerate ORS
Avoid metronidazole unless protozoal infection confirmed
sections.p: Rehydration first, then antibiotics for moderate‑severe disease or high‑risk travelers. Choose agents safe in low‑resource settings.

b: If symptoms persist >48 h after antibiotics, reconsider diagnosis or resistance
Vaccinate against cholera and typhoid where indicated
Teach proper hand hygiene, boiled or filtered water, peeled fruits
sections.p: Re‑assess hydration status after 4‑6 h; advise on safe food and water practices for future travel.

b: Inflammatory bowel disease – chronic course, weight loss, extra‑intestinal signs
Clostridioides difficile infection – recent antibiotics, pseudomembranous colitis
Food poisoning (pre‑travel) – short incubation, resolves within 24 h
sections.p: Conditions that mimic traveller’s diarrhoea but have different management.

b: Negative stool culture does not exclude ETEC (requires special media)
Normal leukocyte count does not rule out invasive bacteria in early disease
sections.p: Laboratory findings may be falsely reassuring.
